title: AWS network services: VPC, security, Route 53 and connectivity
learningObjective: Identify VPC components, understand security groups and network ACLs (plus Inspector), describe Route 53, and choose connectivity options such as VPN and Direct Connect.
foundation: Amazon VPC is your own isolated network in AWS, divided into subnets in different AZs.
Security groups act as firewalls for instances (stateful, allow rules only); network ACLs filter traffic at the subnet level (stateless, allow and deny rules).
Route 53 is AWS's DNS service. Connect your office or data center with AWS VPN (encrypted over the internet) or AWS Direct Connect (private dedicated connection).
engineer: VPC components: CIDR block, subnets (public: route to an internet gateway; private: no direct internet route), route tables, internet gateway, NAT gateway (outbound internet for private subnets), VPC endpoints/PrivateLink, VPC peering, Transit Gateway, Elastic IPs.

Security groups: attached to ENIs/instances, allow rules only, stateful (return traffic allowed). Network ACLs: per subnet, numbered allow/deny rules evaluated in order, stateless (allow ephemeral ports for responses). Amazon Inspector checks network reachability and vulnerabilities; AWS Network Firewall adds managed stateful inspection.
Amazon Route 53: domain registration, DNS hosting, health checks, routing policies (simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity, multivalue).

Connectivity: AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Client VPN, AWS Direct Connect (dedicated or hosted connections; consistent latency; not encrypted by default), AWS Global Accelerator, CloudFront, API Gateway.

example.title: A standard two-tier VPC
body: Web servers sit in public subnets in two AZs behind an ALB; databases sit in private subnets with no internet route, reaching updates through a NAT gateway. Security groups allow 443 to the ALB and only the ALB's security group to the web servers. Route 53 latency routing sends users to the nearest Region; the head office connects with Direct Connect plus a VPN backup.

prerequisites: An AWS account (use an IAM Identity Center user, not root)
permissions: Read-only access to explore; least-privilege permissions to change resources
limits: Conceptual objective: explore in the console; no configuration limits are tested
portal: VPC > Your VPCs > Create VPC (VPC and more).

troubleshooting.symptom: Instance unreachable although the SG allows 443.
troubleshooting.cause: No IGW route or public IP, or NACL blocking.
troubleshooting.fix: Check route table, public IP and NACL in/out rules.

comparisons.difference: NSGs are stateful with allow and deny rules and priorities; AWS splits into stateful allow-only SGs and stateless NACLs.

architectureDecisions: Use private subnets for data tiers; restrict SGs by referencing other SGs.

walkthrough.subtitle: Build a private network for a web app, lock it down, give it a name, and connect the office.
learn: Security groups vs network ACLs (and Amazon Inspector)
Connecting to AWS: VPN and Direct Connect

steps.label: Private network
steps.title: Your app needs its own network
body: Your web servers must be reachable from the internet, but the database must not be. The office also needs a private connection.
On AWS this starts with a VPC.

steps.label: VPC + subnets
steps.title: A VPC with public and private subnets
body: An Amazon VPC is your own isolated network in a Region. You split it into subnets, each in one AZ.
A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway; put load balancers there. A private subnet doesn't; put the app and database there.

callout.text: A NAT gateway in the public subnet lets private instances reach the internet for updates without being reachable from it.

steps.label: Firewalls
steps.title: Two firewalls: security groups and NACLs
body: Security groups protect instances. They only allow traffic (no deny rules) and are stateful: replies are automatically allowed.
Network ACLs protect whole subnets. They allow and deny traffic and are stateless: return traffic needs its own rule.

callout.text: Security group = instance, allow-only, stateful. NACL = subnet, allow + deny, stateless.

steps.label: Inspector
steps.title: Check for weaknesses
body: Amazon Inspector scans your EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure.
Firewalls control traffic; Inspector tells you what's still exposed or out of date.

steps.label: Route 53
steps.title: Route 53 gives the app a name
body: Amazon Route 53 is AWS's DNS service. It translates shop.example into an IP address, can register domain names, checks endpoint health, and can route users by latency, location or weight, or fail over to a backup.

steps.label: Connect office
steps.title: Connect the office privately
body: AWS Site-to-Site VPN creates an encrypted tunnel over the internet. It's quick to set up and cheaper.
AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated private connection from your data center to AWS that doesn't use the public internet. It gives more consistent performance and takes longer to set up.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Network, guards, name, link
body: Public in front, private behind, with guards at each level.
recap: VPC = your network; subnets per AZ; internet gateway for public subnets
Security groups (instance, stateful) and NACLs (subnet, stateless)
VPN over the internet vs Direct Connect private line
